tasks.title: Task 1 · Travel to work
tasks.prompt: The table shows the percentage of commuters in one city who travelled by car, bus, bicycle and on foot in 2010 and 2020. Car: 52%, 42%; bus: 23%, 26%; bicycle: 8%, 17%; on foot: 17%, 15%. Summarise the main features and make relevant comparisons.
tasks.sample: The table compares how commuters in one city travelled to work in 2010 and 2020. Overall, driving remained the most common mode, although its share fell considerably. The largest gain was recorded by cycling, while the proportions travelling by bus and on foot changed less substantially. In 2010, cars accounted for just over half of all trips, at 52%, compared with 23% for buses. By 2020, the figure for driving had declined by ten percentage points to 42%, while bus use had risen by three points to 26%. As a result, the gap between the two modes narrowed from 29 to 16 points. The share of bicycle trips more than doubled, rising from 8% to 17%. Walking moved in the opposite direction, falling slightly from 17% to 15%. Cycling therefore overtook walking by the end of the period, despite having started as the least common option among the four modes shown.

tasks.title: Task 2 · Car-free centres
tasks.prompt: Some people believe that city centres should be closed to private cars. Others argue that this would make city centres less accessible. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
tasks.sample: Whether to restrict private cars in city centres depends on how people currently reach these areas and what alternatives are available. I support phased restrictions when cities can provide viable routes for people whose journeys would otherwise become difficult. Advocates point to competing uses of scarce urban space. A street designed mainly for through traffic can be noisy and difficult to cross, even when it is lined with shops and public services. Removing that traffic can create room for wider pavements, quicker bus routes and outdoor seating. A practical benefit is that a short trip across the district may become easier on foot than it was by car. However, the costs of a ban would fall unevenly. Someone finishing a late shift outside normal bus hours might lose a reliable way home. People with some mobility impairments may need to park close to a destination, and small firms still require access for deliveries. In districts where public transport is poor, a restriction could therefore make a busy centre more exclusive. The strongest policy would address these needs before cutting general access. Cities could improve evening services, reserve accessible bays and schedule deliveries during quiet hours. They could also trial restrictions on a few streets and track travel times, footfall and feedback from residents. That evidence would help determine where a wider scheme is justified. In my view, restrictions should be judged by the range of people who can reach the centre comfortably. With suitable exemptions and frequent transport, fewer private cars can improve access overall.
